text: As someone academically inclined towards the field of AI, hearing a non-technical perspective was quite interesting and rather refreshing. As a Computer Science and Mathematics major, most of what I hear about AI is in regards to how they work and improving the efficiency and effectiveness of these models. Despite my interest in the technical aspect of the field, I was still aware of the morally grey areas of AI. Attending this talk really helped shape a thorough understanding of how other people view AI, and what measures can be taken to bridge this gap between technical improvement and ethics.

I really liked the concept of HCA - Human Centric AI (one of the key concepts focused by the AI policy). This policy doesn't outright reject AI. The fundamental thing to understand is that AI doesn't inherently go against human ethics and morals. It's the way it's been used that is a cause for concern. One of the major issues is the replacement of human labor by AI systems. HCA is focused on coexistence between humans and AI. AI should not be a replacement for humans. It should simply be a tool for increasing efficiency and productivity.

I also found myself agreeing with their take on accountability. They proposed solutions like algorithmic trading, continuous monitoring and lifecycle tracking. By having designated personnel for each part of the pipeline, this helps identify where the problem or misuse occurred, making it easy to punish the wrongdoers. However, I do have a point of contention in regards to this policy. While on paper, this sounds like a great plan, I am wary about the logistics behind enforcing this policy in large AI systems.

One of things from their talk really stood out to me - unethical AI tends to be more profitable. Coupled with rapid advancement in AI, it does seem like it is really hard to come up with regulatory policies that the big companies adhere to. I share their sentiment on having a federal commission to tackle these problems and foster a mutual understanding among all involved to not prioritize advancement over morals and ethics.
